articles.content:
Users of all levels are welcome to ask questions about GNU/Linux and share experiences.

*** Please be civil, notice the "Friendly" in every Friendly GNU/Linux Thread ***

Before asking for help, please check our list of resources.

When answering questions, ask yourself, "Am I answering THEIR question, or explaining MY setup?"

If you would like to try out GNU/Linux you can do one of the following:

0) Install a GNU/Linux distribution of your choice in a Virtual Machine.

1) Install a GNU/Linux distribution of your choice on bare metal

2) Use a live image and to boot directly into the GNU/Linux distribution without installing anything.

Resources: Please spend at least a minute to check a web search engine with your question.

Many free software projects have active mailing lists.

$ man %command%

$ info %command%

$ %command% -h/--help

$ help %builtin/keyword%

Don't know what to look for?

$ apropos %something%

Try a random distro:

https://distrosea.com

https://distro.moe

Every idiot can just shit something out with Claude and post on Twitter with those irritating GPTisms like emojis and so on. God, it pisses me the fuck off.

I'm not even going to get started on ROM Hacking. Over 17 years and it was all for nothing. That fucking shit knows assembly.

articles.content:
New "use-after-free" CVE just dropped.

The victim: TOR browser.

Unfortunately servo is not serviceable yet, so there is no direct full Rust solution.

But if I'm reading this right, this points to a retardation on the TOR browser bundlers part.

How come their bundle doesn't create a sealed network namespace, where the browser itself should be running with no direct or indirect public APIs visible, only a point-to-point veth connection (with no default route or postrouting enabled) to the default (or another) namespace where tor/arti is running?

With this, you get a socks connection only, with no exposure otherwise to the internet, guaranteed at the OS level (unless you have a kernel level container escape exploit at your arsenal, which would be a much bigger deal on its own).

This can be literally done in like 10 lines of shell scripting, including error handling. And it shouldn't have any visible disadvantage to the user (unlike a full container setup, you still have access to your filesystem and all).

Recommendation: Use arti instead of tor (already mature for mere browsing usage), normal Firefox (do lite modification to make it more "secure" if you wish) running in a sealed network namespace as described above (or a fully contained environment if you need that, but you would have been doing that already).

articles.title: Better Languages Give You More
articles.summary:
or, why worse is not better.

Why does /g/ judge programming languages like they’re benchmarking a memcpy implementation? C is a neat wrapper around the machine. Fine. Now look at what Lisp, Smalltalk or Haskell let you build and reason about. Lisp gives you programmable syntax, Smalltalk gives you
articles.content:
or, why worse is not better.

Why does /g/ judge programming languages like they’re benchmarking a memcpy implementation? C is a neat wrapper around the machine. Fine. Now look at what Lisp, Smalltalk or Haskell let you build and reason about. Lisp gives you programmable syntax, Smalltalk gives you a live object world you can inspect and change, and Haskell gives you pure composition backed by a powerful type system. Call this generative coherence: a handful of consistent ideas generate a whole range of useful capabilities. You still have to implement them, but the foundations do much of the conceptual work. “But C is faster” doesn’t answer whether sacrificing those capabilities was worth it.

That’s my problem with treating “worse is better” as an ideal. Making the runtime smaller can mean making every application reinvent what it leaves out. Congratulations, you moved the complexity into everyone else’s code. Speed matters when it enables something you need; it isn’t a universal score for software quality. And today’s implementation overhead isn’t proof of a permanent limit. Better compilers, representations and hardware can reduce it. Build something small and useful, sure, but aim for a coherent foundation that solves several problems together instead of calling every missing feature a victory for simplicity.
